title: The Celtic Path
summary: Thirteen weeks with the gods, the land and the old festivals of Ireland, Scotland, Wales and Gaul: what truly survives, how modern Druids and reconstructionists build on it, and how to keep a Celtic hearth of your own.
welcome:
This journey is for anyone drawn to the Celtic gods, the fire festivals, holy wells and the good folk, whether you lean towards Gaelic reconstructionism, Druidry or a Celtic-flavoured witchcraft. It runs for about thirteen weeks and asks for a little reading, a small hearth shrine and a few minutes most days.

It is honest from the first page: very little survives of pre-Christian Celtic religion, and nearly everything we have was written down by outsiders or by Christian monks. That is not a reason to stop. It is a reason to tread carefully, learn from the living Gaelic and Welsh cultures that kept the old customs, and say clearly which parts are evidence and which are our own building.

At the end you can make a self-dedication. It is not an initiation into a Druid order or a coven, and it does not replace one.
about: There was never one Celtic religion. There were the gods of Gaul, known from Roman-era inscriptions and a few classical writers; the gods of Roman Britain, known from altars and offerings; and the Tuatha Dé Danann of Ireland and the children of Dôn and Llŷr in Wales, known from medieval stories written down centuries after conversion. Running through all of them we find a few steady threads: sacred waters, gifts given to the land, a year turned by fire festivals, and a strong code of hospitality, truth and honour. Today the path has three main branches. Celtic Reconstructionists (often Gaelic Polytheists) work closely from the sources and the living Gaelic cultures. Druids, in orders such as OBOD and ADF, draw on an eighteenth-century revival as well as the older material. And many witches and Wiccans keep a Celtic-flavoured practice inside the Wheel of the Year. This journey shows you all three and tells you plainly where each one stands.
notes: “Celtic” is a language family, not a race or a bloodline. Anyone who comes with respect is welcome on this path, and the app has no place for anyone who says otherwise.

Almost nothing survives of Celtic ritual: no prayers, no liturgy, no description of a rite from the inside. Every rite in this journey is modern, built on the structure of real folk custom, and says so.

Gaelic and Welsh are living languages and cultures, not museum pieces. Many of the customs here were kept by Christian communities who still keep them. Learn from them with gratitude, and never claim their saints, wells or songs as secretly “pagan” property.

The “Celtic tree calendar”, Celtic tree astrology, much of the Druid revival’s lore and the Book of Barddas are modern inventions, some of them deliberate forgeries. They can still be meaningful, but they are not ancient.
The good folk (the sídhe, the aos sí, the Tylwyth Teg) are treated with caution in every culture that remembers them. This journey teaches the old courtesy towards them, not how to summon them.

stages.title: At the threshold
stages.intro: Every Celtic story of the Otherworld begins at an edge: a ford, a mound, a doorway, the shore at dusk. Your journey begins at your own threshold. This first week you set up a simple hearth shrine, make your first offering, and say out loud why you have come.

practices.title: Choose your hearth
practices.instructions: Find a place for a small shrine: a shelf, a windowsill or a corner of the kitchen counter. The hearth was the heart of the Gaelic house, so near the kitchen is ideal. Put down a cloth, a candle or lamp, a bowl for water and a small dish for offerings. If you have a stone, shell or twig from a place you love, add it. Keep it simple for now.
practices.prompt: Why did you choose this spot? What does “hearth” mean in your home now?

practices.title: Visit water
practices.instructions: Some time this week, go to the nearest water you can: a river, a lake, the sea, a canal, even a fountain in a park. Stand there for a few minutes. Notice the sound, the smell, what grows at the edge. You don’t need to do anything else yet. If you can, bring home a little of the water (where it is clean and allowed) for your shrine bowl.
practices.prompt: What did you notice at the water’s edge? Did it feel like a boundary?

rite.title: Kindling at the threshold
rite.summary: A short opening rite in the shape of a Gaelic household blessing: purify, kindle the light, give gifts to the gods, the dead and the spirits of the place, and state your intent.

ingredients.name: A white candle or a small oil lamp
A bowl of clean water (from a river or the sea if you have it, otherwise the tap)
A little milk, butter or cream (or oat milk)
An oatcake or a piece of good bread
A sprig of juniper or rowan

rite.preparation: Tidy and sweep the space first: cleaning the hearth before a feast is one of the oldest Gaelic customs. Wash your hands and face. Turn off your phone. Set the water, candle and offering dish on your shrine, with the milk and bread beside them.

steps.title: Saining
steps.instructions: Dip your fingers in the water and touch your forehead, your lips and your chest. Then sprinkle a few drops around the shrine, moving sunwise (clockwise, deiseal in Irish). If you have juniper, you may instead pass the unlit sprig around the space; the Scottish custom was to burn it, but the scent of the crushed needles is enough indoors.
steps.spoken: Water of the land, wash me clean. Let me come to this hearth with clear eyes and an open hand.

steps.title: Kindle the light
steps.instructions: Light the candle or lamp. Sit with it a moment and let your breathing slow.
steps.spoken: I kindle this light as the hearth was kindled in every house of old: for warmth, for welcome, for the gods.

steps.title: Gifts to the three
steps.instructions: Pour a little milk into the offering dish and break off a piece of bread for each of the three kinds of beings many modern Celtic pagans honour: the gods, the ancestors and the spirits of this place. Speak to each as you give.
steps.spoken:
To the gods of my people and of this land, whose names I am still learning: this is for you.
To the ancestors, of blood and of spirit, who kept the old ways and the old songs: this is for you.
To the spirits of this place, the land under my floor and the water in my pipes: this is for you.

steps.title: State your intent
steps.instructions: In your own words, say why you have come to this path and what you hope to learn over the next three months. Be honest and plain; it is better to say “I don’t know yet” than to promise what you cannot keep.

steps.title: Listen
steps.instructions: Sit in silence for a few minutes. Don’t strain for a sign. Notice what you feel, what you hear in the house, what comes to mind. Write any of it down afterwards.

steps.title: Close with thanks
steps.instructions: Thank each of the three in turn, then snuff the candle (don’t blow it out).
steps.spoken: For what I have been given, my thanks. For what I will learn, my thanks. The hearth is kindled; the road is begun.

rite.closing: Leave the offering on the shrine overnight. In the morning, pour the milk and crumble the bread outside, onto earth or into running water, not down the sink or into the bin. Offerings given to the gods and the good folk are not eaten afterwards.
rite.safety: Never leave a flame unattended, and keep it away from curtains, shelves above and pets’ tails. Don’t burn juniper indoors in a closed room, near birds or anyone with asthma. If you leave milk or bread outdoors, put out only a small amount, away from where it could harm pets or attract pests.

stages.title: Learning the ground
stages.intro: Six weeks of study, about one lesson a week. You will learn who the Celts were, what actually survives, who the gods are, the great texts, the Druids old and new, the modern communities, and the values of hospitality, truth and honour. Read slowly and keep a notebook; this is the foundation for everything after.

lessons.title: Who were the Celts?
lessons.summary: Why “Celtic” is a family of languages and cultures, not a single people, and which branch you are actually working with.

sections.heading: A family of languages
sections.body:
The word Celtic is a modern scholar’s label. Greek writers in the fifth century BCE spoke of the Keltoi, a people living somewhere north of the Mediterranean, but nobody in ancient Ireland or Wales called themselves Celts. The term was revived in 1707, when the Welsh scholar Edward Lhuyd noticed that Irish, Welsh, Breton and the language of ancient Gaul were related and called the family “Celtic”.

So when we say Celtic, we mean people who spoke these languages and shared, more or less, a family of cultures. It is a word about speech and custom, not blood. People of every background have learned these languages and kept these customs, and they belong to anyone who honours them.

sections.heading: The branches
sections.body:
On the Continent there was Gaulish, spoken across what is now France, Belgium and northern Italy, along with Celtiberian in Spain and Galatian as far east as Turkey. These are all extinct, known from inscriptions and names.

In the islands there are two living branches. The Goidelic or Gaelic branch is Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Manx. The Brittonic branch is Welsh, Cornish and Breton (carried to Brittany from Britain in the early Middle Ages). Each has its own gods, stories and folk customs, and they are not interchangeable. The Irish Lugh and the Welsh Lleu are probably related to the Gaulish Lugus, but they are not simply the same god wearing three names.

sections.heading: Hallstatt, La Tène and the archaeology
sections.body:
Archaeologists talk about the Hallstatt culture (roughly 800 to 450 BCE, named after a salt-mining site in Austria) and the La Tène culture that followed it, famous for its swirling, curving art on swords, torcs and mirrors. For a long time these were treated as “the Celts”, spreading out from central Europe. Today many archaeologists are more careful: art styles, languages and peoples don’t always travel together, and the Celtic languages may have spread along the Atlantic coast long before La Tène.

The practical point is simple. When you read a book that talks about “the Celts” believing one thing, ask: which Celts, where, and when? A Gaulish warrior of 100 BCE and a Hebridean grandmother of 1890 lived nineteen centuries apart.

sections.heading: Choosing your thread
sections.body:
Most modern practitioners settle into one culture over time: Irish, Scottish, Welsh, Gaulish or Romano-British. That focus makes the sources manageable and lets you learn a language, a calendar and a set of stories that hang together. Some people do keep a broader “pan-Celtic” practice, and that is a real choice too, as long as you know you are combining things.

You don’t have to decide now. Over the next weeks, notice which stories, landscapes and gods keep catching your attention. That is usually the thread to follow.

knowAndDont.known: The Celtic languages are a well-established branch of Indo-European, with Goidelic (Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Manx) and Brittonic (Welsh, Cornish, Breton) surviving. Classical writers named peoples called Keltoi and Galli, and the Hallstatt and La Tène cultures are well documented by archaeology.
knowAndDont.unknown: How the Celtic languages spread, and how far language, art and identity went together, is still debated. There is no evidence that all Celtic-speaking peoples shared one religion, one pantheon or one sense of being “Celtic”. Modern ideas of a unified Celtic spirituality are a nineteenth- and twentieth-century creation.

lessons.inPractice: Most practitioners pick one culture as their main focus and learn some of its language: a greeting, the names of the festivals, the words for hearth, well and gods. Many keep a small map of their chosen region on or near the shrine.
reflect: Which of the Celtic cultures draws you most, and why? Is it the stories, the landscape, family, or something you can’t name yet?
What did you believe about “the Celts” before this lesson that you now want to check?
further: Barry Cunliffe, The Ancient Celts (2nd ed., 2018)
Simon James, The Atlantic Celts: Ancient People or Modern Invention? (1999)

lessons.title: What survives, and what doesn’t
lessons.summary: The four kinds of evidence (classical writers, archaeology, medieval literature and folklore) and the honest gaps between them.

sections.heading: The outsiders: Greek and Roman writers
sections.body:
The earliest written accounts of Celtic religion come from Greeks and Romans, most of whom were not friends of the people they described. Julius Caesar, who conquered Gaul in the 50s BCE, wrote the longest account in his Gallic War. He tells us the Druids taught that “souls do not become extinct, but pass after death from one body to another”, and that the Gauls “compute the divisions of every season, not by the number of days, but of nights”. That second line is why Celtic festivals are still kept from sunset.

Caesar also tells us about human sacrifice, and he had every reason to make the Gauls look savage. Other writers (Posidonius, through Strabo and Diodorus; Lucan; Pliny the Elder; Tacitus on Anglesey) add details. All of them are useful and all of them must be read with care.

sections.heading: The ground: archaeology and inscriptions
sections.body:
The ground tells a quieter story. In Gaul and Roman Britain there are hundreds of altars and inscriptions naming gods: Sulis at Bath, Coventina at her well on Hadrian’s Wall (where over 13,000 coins were found), Nodens at Lydney, Epona the horse goddess across the empire. The Pillar of the Boatmen, carved in Paris under the emperor Tiberius, shows a horned god labelled Cernunnos.

Above all, archaeology shows the habit of giving precious things to water: swords, shields and cauldrons placed in lakes, rivers and bogs over many centuries, from the Thames to Llyn Cerrig Bach on Anglesey. We may not know the prayers, but we know the gesture.

sections.heading: The monks: medieval Irish and Welsh literature
sections.body: Ireland was never conquered by Rome, and its monks wrote down a huge body of stories, laws, genealogies and place-lore from the seventh century onwards. Wales has the Four Branches of the Mabinogi and the poems of Taliesin. These are our richest sources for the gods, but they were written by Christians, centuries after conversion, who often turned gods into ancient kings, heroes or fairy folk. They are literature, not scripture. They preserve much that is old, and they also invent, rearrange and moralise.

sections.heading: The people: folklore
sections.body: Finally there is folklore: what ordinary people in Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Man and Brittany actually did at Samhain and May Eve, at holy wells and hearths, recorded mostly in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The Irish Folklore Commission collected over a million pages from 1935 onwards. Alexander Carmichael’s Carmina Gadelica gathered Hebridean prayers and charms. These customs are the most practical thing we have, but they were kept by Christian communities, and we can rarely prove which details are pre-Christian.

knowAndDont.known: We have the names of many gods, a great deal of evidence for votive offerings in water and at sacred sites, classical descriptions of the Druids, a rich medieval literature, and well-recorded folk customs for the four festivals, holy wells and the good folk.
knowAndDont.unknown: We have no Celtic prayer, hymn or liturgy from pagan times, no description of a rite written by a participant, and very little on what most gods meant to the people who worshipped them. Every modern Celtic rite fills that gap with reconstruction and creativity, and an honest practitioner says so.

lessons.inPractice: Reconstructionists weigh sources by type and date, and many keep a commonplace book with each idea tagged by where it came from: classical, archaeological, medieval or folk. Druids and Celtic witches usually allow more room for inspiration (often called imbas or awen) but the best still know which is which.
reflect: How do you feel about building a practice on fragments? Is it freeing, unsettling, or both?
Pick one thing you “know” about Celtic religion. Which of the four kinds of source does it actually come from?
further: Julius Caesar, The Gallic War, Book VI.13–18 (public domain, McDevitte & Bohn translation on Project Gutenberg)
Ronald Hutton, Pagan Britain (2013)
Miranda Aldhouse-Green, The Gods of the Celts (1986, reissued)

lessons.title: The gods of many lands
lessons.summary: Gaulish, Romano-British, Irish and Welsh gods, why they don’t form one neat pantheon, and how to begin approaching them.

sections.heading: Gaul and Roman Britain
sections.body:
Caesar said the Gauls worshipped Mercury above all, then Apollo, Mars, Jupiter and Minerva. He was translating, giving Roman names to gods he did not know. Inscriptions give us the native names: Lugus, perhaps the god Caesar called Mercury; Taranis the thunderer; Esus and Teutates, named by the poet Lucan; Sucellus with his hammer and his partner Nantosuelta; Rosmerta of abundance; Belenus of healing; Sequana, goddess of the Seine’s source. Epona the horse goddess was so loved that Roman cavalrymen carried her worship across the empire.

Many of these gods are known from one region, sometimes from one spring. Celtic gods were often gods of a particular place: this river, this hill, this tribe.

sections.heading: The Tuatha Dé Danann of Ireland
sections.body:
In Irish literature the gods appear as the Tuatha Dé Danann, “the peoples of the goddess Danu”, who came to Ireland in mist, defeated the Fomoire, and later withdrew into the mounds (the síd) when the ancestors of the Irish arrived. Among them are the Dagda, the “good god” of the cauldron and the club; Brigid of poetry, healing and smithcraft; Lugh, master of every art; the Morrígan, the great queen of battle and sovereignty; Nuada of the silver arm; Ogma the champion; Dian Cécht the healer; Goibniu the smith; Boann of the river Boyne; and Manannán mac Lir, lord of the sea and the Otherworld isles.

Danu herself is barely attested. Her name is reconstructed from the group name, and a few medieval texts speak instead of Anu, “mother of the gods of Ireland”.

sections.heading: The children of Dôn and Llŷr in Wales
sections.body: In the Welsh Mabinogi the gods have become magicians and rulers of an ancient Britain. The children of Dôn include Gwydion the enchanter and Arianrhod of the silver wheel; Lleu Llaw Gyffes, “the bright one of the skilful hand”, is Arianrhod’s son. The children of Llŷr include Brân the Blessed, whose head kept company with his followers after death, and Branwen. Rhiannon rides out of the Otherworld on a white horse no one can catch, and the story of Ceridwen and her cauldron of inspiration gave us the poet Taliesin. Gwyn ap Nudd, in later lore, leads the Wild Hunt.

sections.heading: Approaching the gods today
sections.body:
Because the evidence is scattered, most practitioners start with one or two gods whose stories they can read and whose land they can connect with, rather than trying to honour a whole pantheon. Read their stories. Learn what they were called in their own language. Find out which places, animals, plants and days belong to them. Then make a small, regular offering and see whether the relationship deepens.

The Living Library has entries for Brigid, the Dagda, Lugh, the Morrígan, Manannán, Cernunnos, Epona, Rhiannon, Arianrhod and Ceridwen, and each has its own journey in the app if one of them calls you.

knowAndDont.known: Hundreds of Gaulish and British divine names survive in inscriptions; the Irish and Welsh literatures describe the Tuatha Dé Danann and the families of Dôn and Llŷr in detail; and a few names (Lugus/Lugh/Lleu, the Matres or mother goddesses, Brigantia/Brigid) appear in more than one region.
knowAndDont.unknown: We cannot be sure how far the medieval Irish and Welsh figures reflect pre-Christian worship; many may be literary creations. Whether Lugh, Lleu and Lugus are one god, how Danu was understood, and whether Cernunnos was worshipped outside Gaul are all open questions. There is no evidence for a “Celtic triple goddess” as a single figure, though triple groupings are common.

lessons.inPractice: Begin by reading one god’s stories and choosing a simple offering for them: milk or butter for Brigid, porridge for the Dagda, a cup of the sea or a bit of seaweed for Manannán. Offer weekly for a month before deciding whether to go further.
reflect: Which god or goddess have you felt drawn to, and what do you actually know about them from the sources?
How do you feel about gods who belonged to one particular river or hill? Who are the gods of the place you live now?
further: Proinsias Mac Cana, Celtic Mythology (1970)
Mark Williams, Ireland’s Immortals: A History of the Gods of Irish Myth (2016)

lessons.title: The great texts
lessons.summary: What the Lebor Gabála, the Mythological and Ulster Cycles, the Mabinogi and the Carmina Gadelica are, and where to start reading.

sections.heading: Ireland: the Book of Invasions and the Mythological Cycle
sections.body:
The Lebor Gabála Érenn, “the Book of the Taking of Ireland”, was compiled in the eleventh century and survives in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster. It tells of six waves of settlers: Cessair, Partholón, Nemed, the Fir Bolg, the Tuatha Dé Danann and finally the sons of Míl, ancestors of the Irish. It is a learned Christian history that slots the gods into a biblical timeline, but it keeps names, places and fragments of verse that are much older.

The richest single story for the gods is Cath Maige Tuired, “the Second Battle of Mag Tuired”. Lugh arrives at Tara and is admitted only when he shows he masters every art; the Dagda meets the Morrígan at a river at Samhain; Nuada gets his silver arm; and the Tuatha Dé defeat the Fomoire and Balor of the evil eye. Add Tochmarc Étaíne (the Wooing of Étaín) and the Dindshenchas, the lore of how places got their names, and you have most of what Ireland tells us of its gods.

sections.heading: Ireland: the heroes
sections.body: The Ulster Cycle centres on the Táin Bó Cúailnge, “the Cattle Raid of Cooley”, with Cú Chulainn defending Ulster against Queen Medb of Connacht. It is a story of heroes, not a religious text, but it is full of geasa (sacred taboos), Otherworld visitors, the Morrígan and the code of honour. The Fenian Cycle of Fionn mac Cumhaill and the voyage tales (Immram Brain, the Voyage of Bran) are where the Otherworld isles shine most brightly.

sections.heading: Wales: the Mabinogi and Taliesin
sections.body:
The Four Branches of the Mabinogi survive in the White Book of Rhydderch (about 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (around 1400). Pwyll trades places with Arawn, king of the Otherworld Annwn, and wins Rhiannon; Branwen is married to the king of Ireland, with tragic results; Manawydan and Rhiannon endure an enchanted, empty land; and Math’s nephew Gwydion conjures Blodeuwedd out of flowers. Lady Charlotte Guest’s translation (1838–49) gave them the name Mabinogion.

The Book of Taliesin holds mysterious poems, and the later Hanes Taliesin (sixteenth century) tells how Gwion Bach tasted three drops from Ceridwen’s cauldron and was reborn as the poet. The Welsh Triads preserve lore in threes.

sections.heading: Scotland: the Carmina Gadelica
sections.body: Alexander Carmichael spent half a century collecting prayers, blessings and charms in the Gaelic-speaking Highlands and Islands, published as Carmina Gadelica from 1900. These are Christian prayers, addressed to the Trinity, Mary, Michael and Brigid as saint, but they show a whole household spirituality: blessings for kindling the fire, milking, weaving, journeys and sleep. The smooring blessing asks “The sacred Three / To save, / To shield, / To surround / The hearth, / The house, / The household”. Carmichael polished some texts, so read him with care, but no single book teaches more about how a Gaelic house prayed.

knowAndDont.known: The manuscripts, their dates and their contents are well established, and good modern translations exist for all the major texts. The Carmina Gadelica is a genuine collection of Highland and Island prayer and lore.
knowAndDont.unknown: How much of the medieval literature reflects pagan belief is disputed: some scholars see deep survivals, others see mostly Christian literary art. Carmichael is known to have edited and “improved” some material. None of these texts is a religious scripture for pagans, and none of them gives us a ritual.

lessons.inPractice: Most practitioners read the stories again and again, like scripture without being scripture. A good start: Cath Maige Tuired, the First Branch of the Mabinogi and a dozen prayers from Carmina Gadelica, read aloud.
reflect: Which story have you read (or now read) that moved you most? What does it seem to say about the gods, or about how to live?
How do you feel about learning from Christian prayers? What would you keep, and what would you change?
further: Jeffrey Gantz (trans.), Early Irish Myths and Sagas (1981)
Sioned Davies (trans.), The Mabinogion (Oxford World’s Classics, 2007)
John T. Koch & John Carey (eds.), The Celtic Heroic Age (4th ed., 2003)
Alexander Carmichael, Carmina Gadelica vol. I (1900, public domain on archive.org)

lessons.title: Druids, then and now
lessons.summary: What the ancient writers said about the Druids, how the revival invented much of modern Druid lore, and the orders that exist today.

sections.heading: The ancient Druids
sections.body:
The Druids were the learned class of Gaul and Britain: priests, judges, teachers and keepers of lore. Caesar says they met each year in the land of the Carnutes, the centre of Gaul, that training could take twenty years, and that they would not write their teachings down. Pliny the Elder describes Druids in white robes cutting mistletoe from an oak with a golden sickle on the sixth day of the moon, and sacrificing two white bulls. Tacitus describes the Roman attack on Anglesey in 60 CE, with Druids raising their hands to the sky.

In Ireland the druí appears in the early laws and stories as a seer, adviser and magician, but by the seventh century the role had faded, and the poets (filid) carried on much of the learning.

sections.heading: The hard question
sections.body: Classical writers say the Druids performed human sacrifice. Some of this is Roman propaganda, but not all of it can be dismissed: bog bodies such as Lindow Man, found in Cheshire in 1984, may have been ritual killings, though the evidence is debated. Honest practitioners don’t deny the question and don’t romanticise it. Modern Druidry rejects any harm to people or animals; the values we keep are the learning, the law and the reverence for nature.

sections.heading: The revival and Iolo Morganwg
sections.body:
From the seventeenth century, antiquarians such as John Aubrey and William Stukeley linked the Druids to Stonehenge and Avebury, monuments in fact about two thousand years older. Fraternal Druid lodges followed, like the Ancient Order of Druids (1781).

The most influential figure was the Welsh stonemason and poet Edward Williams, known as Iolo Morganwg (1747–1826). He held the first Gorsedd of the Bards on Primrose Hill in London in 1792 and created rituals, a Druid prayer, the three-rayed awen symbol and a whole “bardic” philosophy, which he claimed were ancient Welsh tradition. Much of it was his own invention, and some manuscripts were outright forgeries. They were published after his death as Barddas (1862) and shaped Druidry for two centuries. Scholars, notably G. J. Williams in the twentieth century, untangled the forgeries. The Welsh Gorsedd still meets at the National Eisteddfod as a cultural honour, not a pagan rite.

sections.heading: Druid orders today
sections.body:
The Order of Bards, Ovates and Druids (OBOD) was founded in 1964 by Ross Nichols and grew worldwide under Philip Carr-Gomm. It teaches a nature spirituality through three grades (Bard, Ovate, Druid) by correspondence course, with initiations in each, and is open to members of any religion. Ár nDraíocht Féin (ADF, “Our Own Druidism”) was founded in the United States in 1983 by Isaac Bonewits as a more scholarly, explicitly polytheist Druidry drawing on all the Indo-European peoples, with a public Core Order of Ritual and a study programme called the Dedicant Path. Others include the Ancient Order of Druids in America (AODA) and the Henge of Keltria.

Modern Druidry is a living religion in its own right. It simply isn’t a continuation of the ancient Druids, and the good orders say so.

knowAndDont.known: Classical and early Irish sources describe the Druids as a learned, priestly class. The modern revival is well documented, including Iolo Morganwg’s inventions and forgeries, and the founding of OBOD (1964) and ADF (1983).
knowAndDont.unknown: We know almost nothing of what the ancient Druids actually taught, beyond a few classical summaries. Nothing in modern Druid ritual descends from them in an unbroken line, and claims of secret survival are not supported by evidence.

lessons.inPractice: Many people combine Druidry with a Celtic focus: OBOD members often work with Welsh and British lore, ADF groves with Irish, Gaulish or other hearth cultures. If you want initiation or a structured course, an order is the way to get it; this journey does not replace one.
reflect: Does knowing that much Druid lore was invented in the eighteenth century change how you feel about it? Can something be both modern and sacred?
What draws you to the idea of the Druid: the priest, the poet, the judge, the seer, the lover of trees?
further: Ronald Hutton, Blood and Mistletoe: The History of the Druids in Britain (2009)
Philip Carr-Gomm, Druid Mysteries (2002)
Isaac Bonewits, Bonewits’s Essential Guide to Druidism (2006)

lessons.title: Reconstructionists, Druids and Celtic witches
lessons.summary: The main modern ways of being a Celtic pagan, how they differ, and some popular ideas to treat with caution.

sections.heading: Celtic Reconstructionism
sections.body:
Celtic Reconstructionism (CR) grew in the late 1980s and 1990s among people who wanted a practice grounded as closely as possible in the evidence and the living cultures. Many now prefer the name Gaelic Polytheism for the Irish, Scottish and Manx side. Its hallmarks: learning a Celtic language, studying the sources critically, keeping the festivals by their folk customs, honouring gods, ancestors and spirits of place, and supporting the Gaelic and Welsh language communities.

CR is not anti-creativity, but it asks that new practice be in keeping with the old, and marked as new. It tends to avoid casting circles, calling quarters and the god-and-goddess duotheism of Wicca. Groups are small and often online; the CR FAQ, written collectively in 2007, is a good introduction.

sections.heading: Druidry
sections.body: Druid orders draw on the revival as well as the older sources. OBOD rituals take place in a circle and honour the eight festivals of the modern Wheel of the Year; ADF rituals work at a fire, a well and a tree, open a gate to the Otherworld, honour the Three Kindreds (gods, ancestors and nature spirits) and take an omen. Druids tend to welcome inspiration and personal experience more freely than reconstructionists, and many are less concerned with one specific culture.

sections.heading: Celtic-flavoured Wicca and witchcraft
sections.body: Wicca took several of its sabbat names from the Gaelic festivals, and many witches work with Brigid, the Morrígan or Cernunnos inside a Wiccan framework of circle, quarters, God and Goddess. This is a legitimate modern practice. The honest thing is to recognise it as Wicca with Celtic elements, not as “the old Celtic religion”, and to learn the gods’ own stories rather than reducing them to a maiden, mother or crone.

sections.heading: Ideas to treat with caution
sections.body:
A few popular notions come from modern books, not from the Celts. The “Celtic tree calendar” of thirteen tree-months was devised by Robert Graves in The White Goddess (1948), building on a seventeenth-century misreading of the ogham alphabet; Celtic tree astrology came later still. Ogham itself is real, carved on hundreds of stones from the fourth to seventh centuries, and medieval scholars linked its letters to trees, but its use for divination is modern. “Celtic shamanism” is a modern synthesis. And the eightfold “Celtic” Wheel of the Year with solstices and equinoxes is a twentieth-century combination; the Gaelic year had four fire festivals, and the solstices and equinoxes are barely mentioned.

None of this makes these things wrong to use. It means saying where they come from.

knowAndDont.known: Celtic Reconstructionism, Druidry and Celtic-flavoured Wicca are all well-documented modern movements with distinct methods. The origins of the tree calendar (Graves, 1948) and of the eight-festival Wheel (mid-twentieth-century Wicca and Druidry) are well established.
knowAndDont.unknown: There is no way to know whether ancient Celtic peoples used ogham for divination, how they marked the solstices, or whether anything like a circle-casting existed. Each modern community fills these gaps differently, and none can claim to have recovered the original.

lessons.inPractice: Many people move between these approaches over a lifetime. Reconstructionists often join language classes; Druids join an order’s course and local grove; Celtic witches study the gods’ myths alongside their craft. All three can keep the hearth, the festivals and the offerings in this journey.
reflect: Which of the three approaches feels most like home right now? What draws you, and what makes you hesitate?
Is there a practice you love that you now realise is modern? How do you want to hold it?
further: Kathryn Price NicDhàna, Erynn Rowan Laurie et al., The CR FAQ (2007)
Erynn Rowan Laurie, Ogam: Weaving Word Wisdom (2007)
Ronald Hutton, The Stations of the Sun (1996)

lessons.title: Hospitality, truth and honour
lessons.summary: The values at the heart of early Irish and Welsh society, and how to live them now.

sections.heading: Hospitality
sections.body:
In early Ireland, hospitality was law as well as custom. Certain landholders, the briugu or hospitallers, were bound to keep open house for any traveller, and in the stories their hostels stand at crossroads with a cauldron always on the fire. The Triads of Ireland, a collection of wise sayings in threes compiled around the ninth century, name “three caldrons that are in every fort”, one of them “the caldron of guests”. To refuse a guest food was a shame on the household; to harm a guest under your roof was among the worst crimes.

The Triads also list “three prohibitions of food: to eat it without giving thanks, to eat it before its proper time, to eat it after a guest.” The guest is served first, and thanks are given before eating.

sections.heading: Truth
sections.body:
Early Irish wisdom texts put truth at the centre of the world. The Audacht Morainn, “the Testament of Morann”, a seventh-century advice text for kings, teaches that it is through the ruler’s truth, fír flathemon, that the land is fruitful, the weather is mild, the cattle give milk and plagues are kept away. A false judgement could blight the land. Truth here means more than not lying: it is being right with the order of things.

Another of the Triads gives us “Three candles that illumine every darkness: truth, nature, knowledge.”

sections.heading: Honour and the face
sections.body:
Every free person in early Ireland had an honour price, lóg n-enech, literally the “price of the face”. If you were insulted, injured or your hospitality was violated, compensation was owed according to your honour price. You could lose honour by lying, by refusing hospitality, by breaking your word or by being satirised by a poet for real wrongdoing. Poets were feared because satire could raise blisters on the face of a stingy king.

The heroes also carried geasa (singular geis), personal taboos that bound them. Cú Chulainn could not eat the flesh of a dog; when he was offered it by hags at the roadside, he faced a choice between two geasa, and broke one, and died soon after. A geis was a sacred obligation, and breaking it had consequences.

sections.heading: Living these values now
sections.body:
You don’t need a hostel at a crossroads. Hospitality today is feeding people, making room, welcoming the stranger, and keeping a small offering for the gods and the dead at your own table. Truth is keeping your word, speaking honestly even when it costs you, and judging fairly. Honour is behaving so that you would not be ashamed to have your actions told in a story.

Many practitioners take on a small personal geis: a promise kept for the sake of the gods, such as never refusing someone food, or always pouring the first drop of a drink for the household spirits. Choose carefully, keep it small and keep it well.

knowAndDont.known: The early Irish laws (the Brehon laws) and wisdom texts such as the Audacht Morainn and the Triads describe hospitality obligations, honour prices, the ruler’s truth and the power of satire in detail. Similar values run through the Welsh laws and the Mabinogi.
knowAndDont.unknown: These texts were written in Christian Ireland and describe an aristocratic society; we cannot be sure how far they reflect pre-Christian religion, or how ordinary people lived them. Modern “Celtic virtues” lists (for example ADF’s nine virtues) are modern syntheses, though grounded in these sources.

lessons.inPractice: Pour the first of each meal or drink for the gods, the dead or the house before eating. Keep your word, and make amends quickly when you fail. Some keep a written vow or geis on their shrine, renewed each Samhain.
reflect: Who in your life practises real hospitality? What would it mean for you to keep “the caldron of guests” on the fire?
Is there a promise you could make to the gods as a small geis, one you are sure you can keep for a year?
further: Kuno Meyer (trans.), The Triads of Ireland (1906, public domain; on CELT, University College Cork)
Fergus Kelly, A Guide to Early Irish Law (1988)
Fergus Kelly (ed. & trans.), Audacht Morainn (1976)

practices.title: Weekly offering at the hearth
practices.instructions: Once a week, on a day you choose, light your hearth candle and make a small offering: milk, butter, bread, oats, or a drop of ale or whiskey (water, milk or apple juice if you don’t drink). Speak to the gods, the ancestors or the spirits of place, or to a single god you are learning about. Read aloud a short passage from the week’s text.
practices.prompt: What did you offer, to whom, and what did you read? Did anything stand out?

practices.title: A word a week
practices.instructions: Learn one or two words of Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Welsh each week, connected to what you are studying: tine (fire), tobar (well), teallach (hearth, Scottish Gaelic), aelwyd (hearth, Welsh), fáilte (welcome), fírinne (truth). Use them in your prayers. Free courses exist online for all three languages.
practices.prompt: Which word did you learn, and how does it feel to say it at the hearth?

stages.title: Keeping the hearth
stages.intro: Four weeks of practice. Now you put the learning into your hands: a daily hearth rite, offerings to land, sea and sky, the old courtesy towards the good folk, and the customs of the four fire festivals. Do the practices even on days when you don’t feel much. That is how a tradition is kept.

lessons.title: The hearth and the shape of a rite
lessons.summary: How to set up a Celtic hearth shrine, the daily kindling and smooring prayers, and the basic shape of a modern Celtic rite.

sections.heading: The hearth at the centre
sections.body:
In a Gaelic or Welsh house the fire was rarely allowed to go out. In the morning the embers were raked up and the fire kindled; at night it was smoored, covered with ashes so it would smoulder till morning. Carmichael describes Hebridean women laying the embers in a circle, dividing it into three with peats, and covering it while praying. These were daily acts of devotion carried out in the most ordinary room in the house.

You probably don’t have a peat fire, but you can keep a hearth. A candle, an oil lamp or even an electric flame on your shrine stands for it. Light it in the morning, and “smoor” it at night with a short prayer, snuffing it or covering it.

sections.heading: Setting up your shrine
sections.body:
A simple Celtic shrine needs: a light (the hearth), a bowl of water (the well), and something of the land, such as a stone, a branch or a dish of earth from a place you love. Many people add a small image or symbol of a god (a Brigid’s cross, a horse for Epona, a shell for Manannán), a photograph or object for the ancestors, and an offering dish.

Some follow the ADF pattern of fire, well and tree: the fire carries offerings up to the gods, the well reaches down to the ancestors and the deep places, and the tree, or a branch, joins them. That is a modern framework, not an ancient one, but it is practical and beautiful. Keep it clean, dust it weekly and replace water and offerings before they spoil.

sections.heading: The smooring blessing
sections.body:
One of the Hebridean smooring prayers Carmichael recorded runs:

“The sacred Three / To save, / To shield, / To surround / The hearth, / The house, / The household, / This eve, / This night, / Oh! this eve, / This night, / And every night, / Each single night.”

The Three here is the Christian Trinity. Some Christian and Celtic-minded witches keep the prayer as it is; many Celtic pagans adapt it, asking a trio of their own gods, or Brigid of the hearth, to guard the house. Either way, the shape is the gift: a simple, rhythmic blessing that wraps the home for the night.

sections.heading: The shape of a basic rite
sections.body:
Since no pagan Celtic rite survives, modern rites borrow their shape from folk practice and from other Indo-European religions. A sound, simple pattern is: cleanse yourself and the space with water (and juniper, in the Scottish saining tradition); kindle the fire; greet the beings you are honouring, often the gods, the ancestors and the spirits of place; give your offering and say why; listen, or take an omen if you practise divination; give thanks; and close.

ADF’s public Core Order of Ritual is a longer version of the same pattern, adding an honouring of the Earth Mother, the opening of gates to the Otherworld with a gatekeeper (often Manannán), and a “return flow” of blessing from the gods. You can start small and grow.

knowAndDont.known: The Carmina Gadelica and Irish and Welsh folklore record rich hearth customs: kindling and smooring prayers, the fire never allowed to go out, and many prohibitions about giving fire out of the house on certain days.
knowAndDont.unknown: We do not know what pre-Christian household religion looked like or whether the hearth prayers have pagan roots. The fire-well-tree arrangement and the Three Kindreds are modern frameworks (largely from ADF), drawing on Indo-European comparison rather than direct Celtic evidence.

lessons.inPractice: Light your hearth candle each morning with a short greeting and smoor it each night with a blessing. Make a fuller offering weekly and at the festivals. Keep a dish for the gods and one for the ancestors if you can.
reflect: What does your shrine look like now? What do you want to add, and what could you take away?
How did it feel to say a blessing over your home at night? Did you keep the Christian words, change them, or write your own?
further: Alexander Carmichael, Carmina Gadelica vol. I, “Labour” section (1900, public domain)
F. Marian McNeill, The Silver Bough, vol. 1 (1957)
ADF, Our Own Druidry (2009)

lessons.title: Land, sea and sky: offerings and holy wells
lessons.summary: What to offer, how and where; the three realms; and the etiquette of holy wells.

sections.heading: The three realms
sections.body:
Early Irish texts often speak of the world as land, sea and sky. Ulster heroes in the Táin swear to keep their word unless the sky falls on them, the earth opens beneath them, or the sea rises over them; an oath by the whole of the world. Many modern Celtic pagans build on this: they honour the land beneath (where the ancestors and the síd lie), the sea around (the boundary, Manannán’s realm) and the sky above (the gods of light and weather), with the sacred fire at the centre.

This is a modern framework built from a real pattern of speech, not an attested ancient cosmology, but it is a good one. It reminds you that the whole world is involved when you make a promise.

sections.heading: What to offer
sections.body:
The best offerings are the good things of a Celtic farm: milk, cream and butter (the first of the churning was given to the good folk in folk custom), oatcakes, bread, porridge, honey, apples, ale, mead and whiskey. Archaeology shows the ancients gave their finest metalwork to the waters; today a coin or a small handmade object can carry that tradition, but think about where it goes.

Give the first and best portion, not leftovers. Say what you are giving and to whom. Give to fire by burning a small portion (in a fireplace, fire pit or a heatproof dish with a little bread or butter on a tea light), to water by pouring or placing it, or to earth by burying it or setting it under a tree.

sections.heading: Holy wells
sections.body:
There are around three thousand holy wells in Ireland, and many more across Scotland, Wales, Cornwall and Brittany. Most are now dedicated to saints, Brigid above all, and many had pagan predecessors, though that is rarely provable. On the saint’s day (the pattern, from patrún) people come to make the rounds: walking sunwise around the well a set number of times, praying at each station, drinking or washing with the water, and leaving a small token. (Today most well water is untested; wash with it rather than drink it.)

Visit with respect: these are living Christian sites, cared for by local people. Walk the rounds sunwise, take only a little water if any, and don’t leave synthetic rags, plastic or anything that won’t rot. If you tie a cloth to a rag tree (a clootie in Scotland), use undyed cotton or wool and a short strip. Leave the place cleaner than you found it.

sections.heading: What not to do
sections.body: Don’t eat offerings given to the gods, the dead or the good folk; in Irish custom such food was considered taken. Don’t throw coins into rivers or wells that are fragile or protected; many wells now ask people not to. Don’t leave food where it will harm wildlife or pets: no chocolate, grapes, raisins, onion or garlic. And don’t offer what isn’t yours to give: an offering is a gift, and a gift stolen or borrowed shames the giver.

knowAndDont.known: Archaeology shows centuries of votive deposits in water. Thousands of holy wells are documented, with well-recorded rounds, patterns and rag trees. Folk customs of giving milk and butter to the good folk are widely recorded in Ireland and Scotland.
knowAndDont.unknown: We cannot say for certain what the ancient deposits meant, which wells were sacred before Christianity, or whether the three realms were a religious cosmology or simply a way of saying “everything”. Modern offering practices fill these gaps.

lessons.inPractice: Make a small weekly offering at your shrine and dispose of it respectfully outside. Once in this stage, visit a holy well or a spring if you can reach one; otherwise, give an offering to the nearest natural water.
reflect: Which realm, land, sea or sky, feels closest to you? Where in your area can you meet each one?
What can you give that is truly yours: something you made, grew, cooked or saved for?
further: Walter L. Brenneman & Mary G. Brenneman, Crossing the Circle at the Holy Wells of Ireland (1995)
Patrick Logan, The Holy Wells of Ireland (1980)

lessons.title: The Otherworld and the good folk
lessons.summary: The síd, Tír na nÓg and Annwn; who the aos sí are in Gaelic and Welsh tradition; and the old courtesy towards them.

sections.heading: The Otherworld
sections.body:
Irish and Welsh stories are full of an Otherworld that lies very close: inside the mounds, beneath lakes, across the sea in the west or simply through a mist that falls on the road. In Ireland it has many names: Tír na nÓg (the Land of the Young), Mag Mell (the Plain of Delight), Emain Ablach (the Isle of Apples). In Wales it is Annwn, ruled in the First Branch by Arawn. Time runs differently there; Oisín returns from Tír na nÓg to find three hundred years have passed.

The Otherworld comes nearest at the edges: at dusk and dawn, at fords and shores, at Samhain and May Eve.

sections.heading: The good folk
sections.body:
After the Tuatha Dé Danann withdrew into the síd, they became the aos sí, “the people of the mounds”. Most people who believed in them avoided naming them directly. In Ireland they were the Good People (na daoine maithe), the Gentry, the Other Crowd or simply Them; in Scotland the Good Neighbours or the people of peace; in Wales the Tylwyth Teg, the Fair Family, or Bendith y Mamau, the Mothers’ Blessing. Those polite names are a clue: you speak well of them because they are not always well-disposed.

They are not small or sweet. Folk tradition credits them with beauty and music, but also with blighting cattle, taking children and leaving changelings, and leading travellers astray. The tales are about respect and caution, not about friendship to be cultivated lightly.

sections.heading: The old courtesy
sections.body:
Rural Irish, Scottish and Welsh families kept a few simple customs. A little milk or the first of the butter was left for the good folk. People warned them before throwing water out at night, in case they were passing. Lone hawthorns and ringforts (raths and lios) were left alone; even modern road-builders in Ireland have rerouted around fairy bushes. Food that had fallen on the floor or been left out on Samhain night was considered theirs. Iron, rowan, salt and a red thread were traditional protections. Thanks were not always spoken directly, for fear of seeming to settle a debt.

You can keep these customs as a matter of good neighbourliness: leave the lone thorn alone, don’t take stones from ringforts, be polite to the land, and keep a small offering for the spirits of place.

sections.heading: What this journey won’t teach
sections.body: Some modern books treat the good folk as spirit guides to call up or contract with. The folk tradition would think that very unwise. This journey keeps to the courtesy and the protections, not summoning. If you feel drawn to deeper Otherworld work, learn first from people who have done it in a careful tradition, and ward yourself before you begin.

knowAndDont.known: Belief in the good folk is richly documented in Irish, Scottish, Manx and Welsh folklore, with consistent customs: euphemistic names, milk and butter offerings, avoiding fairy forts and thorns, iron and rowan as protection. The medieval literature describes the síd and the Otherworld in detail.
knowAndDont.unknown: Whether the aos sí descend from pre-Christian gods, nature spirits or the dead (the folklore itself mixes all three) is unknown. Modern ideas of fairies as friendly guides owe more to Victorian art and New Age writing than to Gaelic tradition.

lessons.inPractice: Many Celtic pagans keep a small dish for the spirits of place, separate from the gods’ offerings. Some hang a rowan cross with red thread or keep iron by the door. When walking in wild places, they greet the land and leave it as they found it.
reflect: What stories of the good folk do you know, from books or from your own family? What do they teach about boundaries?
How will you show courtesy to the spirits of the place where you live?
further: W. Y. Evans-Wentz, The Fairy-Faith in Celtic Countries (1911, public domain)
Lady Augusta Gregory, Visions and Beliefs in the West of Ireland (1920, public domain)
Eddie Lenihan & Carolyn Eve Green, Meeting the Other Crowd (2003)

lessons.title: The dark half: Samhain and Imbolc
lessons.summary: The real folk customs of Samhain and Lá Fhéile Bríde, and how to keep them today.

sections.heading: The Gaelic year
sections.body: The Gaelic year turned on four festivals, each beginning at sunset: Samhain (1 November), Imbolc (1 February), Bealtaine (1 May) and Lughnasadh (1 August). The tale Tochmarc Emire (the Wooing of Emer) lists all four with a learned gloss on each, calling the August feast by its older name Brón Trogain, and notes that the year once had two halves, summer from Bealtaine and winter from Samhain. They were legal and agricultural turning points, when rents were paid, livestock moved and hired workers changed masters. The Gaulish Coligny calendar, a bronze tablet of the second century CE found in France in 1897, marks a month called Samonios with “three nights” (TRINOX SAMONI), which may or may not be related to Samhain.

sections.heading: Samhain
sections.body:
Samhain, “summer’s end”, opened the dark half of the year, and many people call it the Gaelic new year, though that is a reasonable reading rather than a stated fact in the sources. In the stories it is when the síd mounds open, when great assemblies were held at Tara, and when the Dagda met the Morrígan. In folk custom, recorded across Ireland, Scotland and Man, people lit bonfires, went guising in masks and disguises, carved turnips into lanterns, played divination games with apples and nuts, and baked barmbrack with a ring inside to foretell a marriage. Food was left out and doors left unlatched for the dead coming home. After Samhain the blackberries were left alone; the púca had spoiled them. In Wales, Nos Galan Gaeaf was a spirit night (ysbrydnos), with bonfires and a fearsome tailless black sow said to take the last one home.

Today you can keep it with a meal for the living and the dead: a candle in the window, a plate set for the ancestors, the names of your dead spoken aloud, apples and nuts on the table. If a death is recent and raw, keep it as lightly as you need to, and lean on the living too: friends, a bereavement service or your doctor.

sections.heading: Imbolc and Lá Fhéile Bríde
sections.body:
Imbolc (also called Oimelc, often explained as “ewe’s milk”) marked the first stirrings of spring and became the feast of St Brigid. Carmichael recorded Hebridean women making a sheaf of oats into the figure of Bride, laying it in a basket-bed, and calling at the door: “Bride’s bed is ready.” Another answered, “Let Bride come in. Bride is welcome.” In Ireland, crosses were woven from rushes and hung over the door; a cloth or ribbon (the brat Bríde) was left outside overnight for Brigid to bless, then used for healing through the year; the Brídeóg, a doll of Brigid, was carried from house to house. At Kildare, Gerald of Wales recorded in the twelfth century that nuns kept a perpetual fire for her, and since 1993 the Brigidine Sisters have tended a flame there again. Since 2023, St Brigid’s Day has been a public holiday in Ireland.

Brigid is both goddess and saint, and many Irish people honour the saint with deep love. Keep her day gently: weave a cross, leave the brat out, bless water for your shrine.

sections.heading: Keeping them now
sections.body: Keep each festival from sunset on the eve. Clean the house and shrine beforehand, as Gaelic households did. Make an offering, share a meal and do at least one real folk custom rather than a generic ritual. If you live in the southern hemisphere, most Celtic pagans keep the festivals by season (Samhain on 30 April–1 May), but some keep the northern dates; choose and be consistent.

knowAndDont.known: Samhain and Imbolc are named in medieval Irish literature, and their folk customs (guising, bonfires, apple and nut divination, food for the dead, Brigid’s crosses, the brat Bríde, the Brídeóg) are richly documented from the eighteenth to twentieth centuries.
knowAndDont.unknown: There is no direct evidence that Samhain was a festival of the dead in pagan times, or that Imbolc honoured a goddess Brigid before it honoured the saint. The link between the Gaulish Samonios and Samhain is uncertain. “Celtic New Year” at Samhain is a reasonable reading, not a proven fact.

lessons.inPractice: At Samhain: a candle in the window, a plate for the dead, apples and nuts, and naming your ancestors. At Imbolc: weave a rush or straw cross, leave a cloth out overnight, bless water and welcome Brigid at the door.
reflect: Who will you remember by name at Samhain? What food would they want?
What is waking in your life as winter loosens? What would you ask Brigid to bless?
further: Kevin Danaher, The Year in Ireland (1972)
Ronald Hutton, The Stations of the Sun (1996)
Alexander Carmichael, Carmina Gadelica vol. I, “Seasons” (1900, public domain)

lessons.title: The bright half: Bealtaine and Lughnasadh
lessons.summary: May Eve fires, dew and the May bush; the hill-top gatherings and first fruits of Lughnasadh.

sections.heading: Bealtaine
sections.body:
Bealtaine (Calan Mai in Wales) opened the bright half and summer pasture. Cormac’s Glossary, around 900 CE, says the Druids lit two fires with incantations and drove the cattle between them to protect them from disease. Fires were lit on hills into modern times, and at the Hill of Uisneach the Bealtaine fire has been revived in recent years. In folk custom, May Eve was dangerous: the good folk were moving, and butter, milk and luck could be stolen. People hung rowan over doors and byres, put primroses and marsh marigolds on thresholds, and would not give fire, milk or salt out of the house on May Day.

On May morning girls washed their faces in the dew for beauty. A May bush (often a hawthorn branch, or a small tree) was decorated with ribbons and eggshells outside the house; but whitethorn blossom was widely thought unlucky to bring indoors.

sections.heading: Lughnasadh
sections.body:
Lughnasadh, the festival of Lugh, came at the start of the harvest. Medieval texts tell that Lugh founded the gathering at Tailtiu in honour of his foster-mother, who died clearing the plains of Ireland for farming. The Óenach Tailten included games, markets, law, horse races and marriages. In her classic study The Festival of Lughnasa (1962), Máire MacNeill found the festival still alive at nearly two hundred sites: people climbed hills and gathered at lakes on the last Sunday of July or first of August, picked bilberries (fraughans), danced, matched couples, and ate the first new potatoes. Reek Sunday pilgrimage up Croagh Patrick and the Puck Fair at Killorglin, where a wild goat is crowned king, both keep the season.

In Wales it is Gŵyl Awst, and in England the Christian Lammas, the loaf-mass, offered the first bread of the harvest.

sections.heading: Keeping them now
sections.body: At Bealtaine: gather a little hawthorn or rowan (from a tree that has plenty, with thanks), make a May bough for your door, rise early to wash in the dew, and light a candle or a small safe fire for protection over the summer. At Lughnasadh: climb a hill if you can, pick wild berries, bake bread from new flour and give the first piece to Lugh and the land, and hold games or a small gathering. Lughnasadh is also a good time to honour the hard work behind every harvest: farmers, workers and those who feed you.

sections.heading: The festivals and the Wheel
sections.body: Wiccans and Druids keep these four alongside the solstices and equinoxes in the eight-spoked Wheel of the Year. If you follow that Wheel, the four Gaelic fire festivals are its cross-quarter days. A reconstructionist will usually keep only the four, and mark midsummer with the St John’s Eve fires of folk custom. Either is fine; just know which you are doing.

knowAndDont.known: Bealtaine and Lughnasadh are named in early Irish texts. Cormac’s Glossary describes Bealtaine fires and cattle; the Tailtiu assembly is well attested; and folk customs (May dew, May bushes, rowan, protecting butter and fire; hill gatherings, bilberry picking, Puck Fair) are thoroughly documented.
knowAndDont.unknown: Whether Lugh’s festival was always his, and what the fire rites at Bealtaine meant beyond protecting cattle, are not known. The idea of Bealtaine as a fertility rite of a god and goddess’s marriage is modern Wiccan theology.

lessons.inPractice: At Bealtaine: dew washing, a May bough at the door and a protection rite for the home. At Lughnasadh: a first-fruits offering of bread or berries, a hill walk and games with friends.
reflect: What do you want to protect as summer opens? What are you harvesting this year, literally or otherwise?
Is there a hill, lake or high place near you that could be your Lughnasadh place?
further: Máire MacNeill, The Festival of Lughnasa (1962)
Kevin Danaher, The Year in Ireland (1972)

practices.title: Kindling and smooring
practices.instructions: Each morning, light your hearth candle with a short greeting. Each night before bed, say a smooring blessing (the Carmina Gadelica words, or your own) and snuff the light. On busy days a single sentence is enough.
practices.prompt: How did the hearth feel today? What did you ask it to guard?

practices.title: Land, sea and sky
practices.instructions: Once a week, make an offering to one of the three realms in turn: bury bread or pour milk on the earth for the land; pour a drink or place flowers in water for the sea; burn a little bread or butter in a safe flame for the sky. In the fourth week, honour all three together.
practices.prompt: Which realm did you honour this week, and how?

practices.title: A visit to a well or spring
practices.instructions: Find a holy well, spring or source near you (there are directories online for Ireland, Britain and Brittany). Visit with respect: walk sunwise around it three times, wash your hands or face in the water, leave nothing that won’t rot. Most holy wells are untested, so don’t drink unless the water is signed as safe. If none is within reach, visit a stream or river.
practices.prompt: What did the place feel like? Who cares for it now?

stages.title: Sitting with it
stages.intro: A week to step back and ask whether this path is yours. There is no wrong answer. The Celtic stories are full of people who turned back at the edge of the Otherworld and were wiser for it. Choosing to pause, to keep going without dedicating, or to follow a different path or god are all good outcomes.

practices.title: A walk to think
practices.instructions: Take a long walk on your own, to water if you can. Don’t try to decide anything. At the end, sit and write down whatever is true for you about this path right now.
practices.prompt: What did the walk tell you? What would you say to the gods if they asked what you want?

questions: Have you kept the hearth most days, and do you want to keep doing it, not because you should but because you would miss it?
Do you feel drawn to particular Celtic gods, a particular land or language, or is it a general feeling? Either is fine, but which is it?
Can you live comfortably with how little survives, and with building practice from fragments and marking it honestly?
Are the values of hospitality, truth and honour ones you want to be held to?
Would you be better served by joining a Druid order, a grove or a reconstructionist group, either instead of or alongside a self-dedication?
Is something else calling louder, another path or another god? It is a good outcome to go and follow it.
Would it be wiser to pause for a season and come back? The hearth will still be here.

stages.title: Dedication at the hearth
stages.intro: If you choose to, you now dedicate yourself to the Celtic path. This is a self-dedication: a promise you make, in your own words, to the gods, ancestors and spirits you have come to know. It is not an initiation. It does not make you a Druid in any order or a member of any coven or grove, and it does not replace OBOD’s grades, ADF’s Dedicant Path or initiation in any tradition that has one. Choose a meaningful day, ideally one of the four fire festivals or a dawn near water.

practices.title: Write your vow
practices.instructions: Before the rite, write your dedication. Keep it short and true: whom you are dedicating to, what you promise (practise at the hearth, keep the festivals, study, live by hospitality, truth and honour), and for how long; a year and a day is traditional in many modern groups. Many people phrase it in threes. Promise only what you can keep. You may include one small geis.
practices.prompt: Read your vow aloud. Does every word feel true?

rite.title: Rite of self-dedication
rite.summary: A dedication at dawn or at the hearth, giving gifts to land, sea and sky, binding a vow in threes, and receiving the blessing of water.

ingredients.name: Your hearth candle or lamp, or a small outdoor fire where it is safe and allowed
A bowl of water, from a well, spring, river or the sea if possible
Three offerings: something for the land (bread, oatcake), the sea (salt, a shell, a drink) and the sky (butter or incense for the fire)
A gift for the gods that you made or chose with care
A cord, ribbon or token to wear or keep (undyed wool, a red thread, a ring)
A sprig of juniper or rowan

rite.preparation: Clean the house and shrine as for a festival. Bathe and dress in clean clothes. Fast lightly if that is safe for you. If you are going outdoors, choose a quiet place by water or on a hill, take everything you need, and plan to leave no trace. At dawn it is colder than you expect: dress warmly, tell someone where you are going, and stay on the shore or bank rather than in the water.

steps.title: Saining
steps.instructions: Wash your hands and face in the water. Walk sunwise around your space three times, sprinkling water. If you have juniper or rowan, carry it with you.
steps.spoken: By water I am cleansed. By the green branch I am guarded. I come clean to the hearth.

steps.title: Kindling
steps.instructions: Light the fire or candle with care and attention.
steps.spoken: I kindle the sacred fire, the hearth at the centre of the worlds. Let my words rise with its light.

steps.title: Honouring land, sea and sky
steps.instructions: Give your three offerings, one at a time. Lay bread on the earth or a dish for the land; pour or set a gift in the water for the sea; place butter or incense on the flame, or near it, for the sky.
steps.spoken:
Land beneath me, home of the ancestors: receive my gift.
Sea about me, the boundary and the road: receive my gift.
Sky above me, the bright road of the gods: receive my gift.

steps.title: Calling the gods, ancestors and spirits
steps.instructions: Greet the beings you have come to know, by name if you have them: your gods, your ancestors, the spirits of your place. Speak warmly, as to honoured guests.

steps.title: The vow
steps.instructions: Hold your gift for the gods in your hands and read your vow aloud. Speak slowly. When you finish, place the gift on the shrine or in the fire or water, as fits it. Then call the three realms as witnesses.
steps.spoken: This is my word, given freely. Let the land, the sea and the sky be witness: I will keep it while the sky stays above me, the earth below me, and the sea about me.

steps.title: Binding
steps.instructions: Tie the cord or ribbon around your wrist, or put on your token, with three knots: one for the gods, one for the ancestors, one for the spirits of place.
steps.spoken: One for the gods. One for the ancestors. One for the land. Bound by my own hand and my own word.

steps.title: The blessing of water
steps.instructions: Dip your fingers in the water and touch your forehead, lips and chest, as in the threshold rite. This time, receive it as a blessing given back.
steps.spoken: As I have given, let me be given to. As I have welcomed, let me be welcome.

steps.title: Listening
steps.instructions: Sit in silence by the fire or the water. If you practise divination (ogham, cards), you may draw one omen and read it gently.

steps.title: Thanks and closing
steps.instructions: Thank each of the beings you called, in reverse order. Smoor or snuff the flame and say your night blessing, even if it is morning.
steps.spoken: For your presence, my thanks. For the road ahead, my thanks. The hearth is kept; the word is given.

rite.closing: Share a meal afterwards, alone or with friends, and set aside the first portion for the gods. Leave the shrine offerings until the next day, then return them to earth or running water. Keep your vow somewhere safe and read it again at Samhain.
rite.safety: Use a fire only where it is safe and legal, with water to hand, and put it out completely. Never leave a candle unattended. Burning juniper or incense makes smoke; do it outdoors or with a window open, away from birds, pets and anyone with breathing problems. Keep salt, butter and bread offerings away from pets, and avoid onion, garlic, grapes, raisins and chocolate in anything left outdoors.

stages.title: The turning year
stages.intro: The dedication is a beginning. Keep the hearth daily, the four fire festivals through the year, and renew your vow each Samhain, the turn into winter that many keep as the Gaelic new year. Keep reading the stories, keep learning the language and keep visiting the waters.

practices.title: Keeping the fire festivals
practices.instructions: At Samhain, Imbolc, Bealtaine and Lughnasadh, keep at least one real folk custom from the lessons, make an offering at sunset on the eve, and share food with someone.
practices.prompt: Which festival was this, what custom did you keep, and what did it teach you?

practices.title: A monthly offering to the land
practices.instructions: Once a month, take an offering to the land or water near your home, and spend a little time there. Pick up litter while you are there: caring for the land is an offering too.
practices.prompt: What changed in the land since last month?

practices.title: Samhain rededication
practices.instructions: Each Samhain, reread your vow. Keep what is still true, change what is not, and renew it in a short version of the dedication rite: water, fire, three gifts, your word, the three knots.
practices.prompt: What have you kept this year, and what do you promise for the next?
